author: stone
topic: AI-assisted nursing notes — 9x faster and one near-miss
anecdote: Built an AI-assisted Python template tool for 12 nursing-note types in a Sydney GP clinic. Iron-infusion record almost shipped without batch number / expiry — caught in cross-check.

author: stone
topic: Writing better patient education handouts with an AI assistant (with my actual prompts)
anecdote: I use the AI for two main handout types: post-procedure care (iron infusion, wound care, suture removal) and chronic disease education (diabetes, hypertension, asthma). The edits I make most often: bringing the reading level down from medical to patient-friendly, adding red-flag warnings the AI tends to omit (for example the line about returning immediately if a wound dressing shows heavy bleeding), and tailoring the language for the literacy mix in our patient pool. The AI gets the structure right; I add the safety net.

author: stone
topic: Building Aura app week 1 — what the AI coding tool got right and what it didn't
anecdote: First commit at 11pm Sunday. By Tuesday the AI coding tool had refactored my auth flow three times. Two were wrong.

author: stone
topic: Why I killed my first nurse-tooling project before I wrote any code
anecdote: I am Stone (AHPRA-registered RN in Sydney primary care, indie dev). I wanted to automate clinical-note workflow at the clinic. The only way to make it actually useful was to read patient data straight from our practice management software. I worked through what that would mean: a third-party tool I built sitting inside the PMS data flow, with patient identifiers passing through. It was a clear breach of patient privacy (Australian Privacy Act 1988 / APPs) and almost certainly of the PMS vendor's terms of service. I killed the project before I wrote the integration code. Sometimes the right move is recognising the rule that means the project cannot exist in this form.

author: megan
topic: Using AI to draft parent communication for a 3-year-old room
anecdote: Megan tried using an AI assistant to draft the weekly parent newsletter. First version was too corporate. Took 4 prompt iterations to sound like her.

author: megan
topic: Documenting child learning observations with AI assist (without losing your voice)
anecdote: Tried the AI on three individual learning observations for under-5s and deleted all three. The most memorable: I asked it to draft an observation aligned with EYLF Outcome 1 for a 4-year-old who had resolved a peer conflict over a toy in outdoor play. The AI returned a sentence about 'the child demonstrated an emerging capacity for self-regulation and prosocial negotiation strategies.' What I had actually seen was the child looking their friend in the eye and saying 'you can have it after I count to five,' then counting out loud on their fingers. The AI wrote the conclusion. I write the moment.

author: stone
topic: When I do not reach for the AI — the cases that need hands not prompts
anecdote: Walk-in patient with sudden central chest pain and diaphoresis. I went straight to ECG, baseline obs, and grabbed the senior nurse — the AI assistant did not come near it. Pulling leads onto a patient and reading a 12-lead is ten times faster than typing a prompt and reading a response. The AI lives in the documentation layer and the patient-education layer; it does not live at the bedside in the first five minutes of a possible cardiac event. Knowing which layer you are in is the actual skill.

author: stone
topic: The clinical topic where the AI was a year behind — and how I caught it
anecdote: Asked the AI for a stepwise asthma management summary I could adapt into a patient handout. The version it produced still leaned on a SABA-only reliever pathway. I cross-checked against the current Australian Asthma Handbook (National Asthma Council Australia) and the GINA 2024 update — both now lead with anti-inflammatory reliever therapy for adults and adolescents. Evergreen clinical topics are the most dangerous AI use case because the AI sounds confident on guidance that has already moved. The fix is a habit, not a feature: every clinical claim gets verified against the current Australian source before it touches a handout.

author: megan
topic: Five curriculum ideas from the AI — why I picked the one tied to our actual yard
anecdote: Asked the AI for theme angles for sustainability with 3-4 year olds. It returned five: water play, recycling craft, garden patch, animal habitat, weather chart. I picked garden patch because our service had just put in a raised bed at the back of the yard, so the children could actually plant, water, and watch something grow over the term. The other four would have been fine on paper and dead in practice — they were not tied to anything the children could touch this week. The AI gave me options; the room and the yard told me which one was real.

author: stone
topic: Why I stripped every AI brand name out of my own blog (after launch)
anecdote: Launched the site, then realised I had named the specific AI brand I use across three published posts, the static pages, the content queue, and even the agent contracts driving the daily publishing pipeline. Ran one pass to replace every mention with 'the AI' or 'the model'. Brand neutrality on a personal blog is not an SEO call. It is a reader-trust call: the moment a reader pattern-matches your essay as marketing for someone else's product, the rest of the newsletter loses authority — even posts that have nothing to do with that tool. The lesson is to decide your brand-name policy before you publish, not after.

author: stone
topic: Why my daily 7am blog cron silently skipped for three days — a launchd throttle bug
anecdote: Set up a macOS launchd LaunchAgent to publish one article every morning at 7am. The first three mornings the cron fired and immediately exited skip, last run 71190s ago. Read: 19.8 hours. My throttle threshold was 22 hours. Daily cadence is 24 hours; any prior run after 9am leaves a gap below 22h, so the next morning is silently skipped. Threshold too close to the daily period had zero safe margin. Fixed by dropping the throttle to 18 hours, which leaves a 6-hour buffer in either direction. The bug was invisible because launchd reported exit 0 and the script's skip-log line looked identical to the success log line at a glance.

author: stone
topic: How my content agent invented a UK nurse persona for a post about my own work
anecdote: Wrote a dev-diary post about killing a clinical-tool side project. Sent the topic line, the author binding (Stone, AHPRA-registered RN, Sydney), and the real anecdote to the content-writer agent. The agent ignored the author binding and wrote the article as Megan — UK NMC-registered, North London NHS, completely fictional. It pattern-matched the word 'nurse' in the topic and reconstructed a persona that fit the surface words. Two fixes stopped the bleed: (1) author binding became a required field on every queue entry, not inferred from niche or topic, and (2) the content-writer contract now has a HARD RULE forbidding persona inference from topic strings. The lesson: when an agent has freedom to fabricate, freedom plus surface words equals fabrication.
